title: Pentecost: The Birth of the Church
lead: God does not leave His disciples alone. He gives the Spirit, who turns fear into courage and makes a handful of people into a community that carries hope.
questions: If someone from far away listened to your church and to you today, would they hear the wonders of God in their own language?
What does your faith lack more, knowledge or fire? When did you last pray for fire?
Who, though far away, has been written into your church’s birth certificate, yet has dropped out of your plans and prayers?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Fifty days after Easter, about a hundred and twenty people are sitting in a house in Jerusalem: the same ones who scattered into the dark on the night of the arrest. They have no program, no budget, no patron. They have been told to wait. This is what the church looks like a few minutes before it is born. The day is no accident. Pentecost was a harvest festival, the day of firstfruits – and it was then that God gathered the first harvest of the new era: three thousand baptized. The roar of wind and the “tongues like flames of fire” are the scenery of Sinai, except that this time the fire did not settle on a mountain no one could approach. It “separated and came to rest on each of them.” God stopped dwelling on a dangerous mountain. He came to live in His people.

Drawn by the noise, a crowd of pilgrims from fifteen nations, which Luke arranges like a compass rose, says in amazement: “we hear them declaring the wonders of God in our own tongues!” In our own tongues, the ones we have known from the cradle. The Spirit’s first gift was speech people could understand without a dictionary, which means that God comes out to meet us, not the other way around. Then a speaker stands up: Peter, a man who had denied his Lord three times, faces a crowd in the city where Jesus was executed. His sermon contains an argument that could be made in no other place: David died, “and his tomb is with us to this day.” Anyone could go and check. So the psalm about the Holy One who would not see decay was speaking about the one whose tomb had been empty for seven weeks. The outpouring of the Spirit, which could be seen and heard, was the physical evidence that Someone had taken the throne.

The crowd asks, “What shall we do?” Peter answers that they must repent and be baptized, and then they will receive the gift of the Spirit. “This promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off.” Into the church’s birth certificate God wrote people who were not yet in the room. Among the baptized were visitors from Rome. Most likely it was they who, when they went back home, carried the gospel to the capital of the empire. The church’s first missionary network turned out to be the roads home of ordinary pilgrims.
The church rarely lacks information or arguments. What it lacks is fire, and we may pray for it, because it has been promised.

Yesterday we talked about the resurrection. Since then fifty days have passed, and ten since the ascension. In a house in Jerusalem there are about a hundred and twenty people: the same disciples who scattered into the dark on the night of the arrest, and the women who had proved more faithful than they were. They have received a promise of power and orders to wait. They have no program, no budget, no structures, and no influential patron. This is what the church looks like a few minutes before it is born: a handful of frightened people behind closed doors. That picture is worth remembering before we see the next one.

sections.heading: The Feast of Firstfruits
paragraphs: The day is no accident. Pentecost, Shavuot in Hebrew, was a harvest festival – people brought the firstfruits to the temple, the first loaves from the new grain, in thanksgiving for the start of the harvest. On that very day God gathered the first harvest of the new era: three thousand baptized by evening. The festival calendar turned out to be prophecy, just as it did with the death of Jesus. Christ was crucified at the feast of Passover, offered up as the perfect Lamb. The way the Spirit comes is significant too: “a sound like a mighty rushing wind” and “tongues like flames of fire.” Wind, roar, and fire are the scenery of Sinai, the mountain where God gave the Commandments out of the fire. Jewish tradition used Shavuot to commemorate the giving of the Law. Except that this time the fire did not settle on the summit of a mountain no one was allowed to climb. It “separated and came to rest on each of them”: on fishermen, on women, on disciples nobody had ever heard of. What had been distant and terrifying at Sinai came to rest, on the day of Pentecost, right on people’s heads. God stopped revealing Himself on an unapproachable mountain and came to live in His people.

sections.heading: Each One Heard His Own Language
paragraphs: The result is immediate and very concrete. Filled with the Spirit, people begin to speak “in other tongues,” and the crowd of pilgrims drawn by the noise is stunned. Luke lists fifteen peoples and regions, and the list is laid out like a compass rose: Parthians, Medes, and Elamites from the east, Cappadocia and Pontus from the north, Egypt and Libya from the south, Rome from the west, plus islanders from Crete and Arabs from the desert. The whole world of the day in a sample. All of them, amazed, repeat the same thing – “we hear them declaring the wonders of God in our own tongues!” In our own tongues. Not in Hebrew, the sacred language of a religion you would first have to climb up to. In their mother tongue, the one known from the cradle, the one people count in, argue in, and dream in. The text also stresses how sober the whole scene is. The speakers are Galileans who had walked with Jesus, the listeners understand the content, and when Peter takes the floor, the others know how to fall silent. This is not a description of ecstasy but of the gospel being proclaimed and reaching everyone. The Spirit’s first gift to the church was the ability to speak about God so that people understood it without a dictionary. This shows the character of God, who comes out to meet people, not the other way around. A church that speaks a jargon only insiders understand is doing something quite different from Pentecost. The rain of the Spirit begins when outsiders understand everything.

sections.heading: Peter, Who Had Denied Him
paragraphs: Someone in the crowd sneers: “They are drunk on new wine!” Then a speaker stands up. The same Peter who some fifty days earlier had denied Jesus three times in front of a servant girl. Now he stands before a crowd of thousands, in the city where Christ was executed, and preaches a sermon about Him. That change by itself is an argument: something must have happened to this man. Peter declared that the prophecy of Joel is being fulfilled: “I will pour out My Spirit on all people.” On all people: on sons and daughters, on young and old, on menservants and maidservants. The prophet promised the Spirit democratically, cutting across every hierarchy of gender, age, and social standing. Peter announces that this is exactly what is happening. Then he builds an argument that could have been made in no other place and at no other time: the patriarch David died, “and his tomb is with us to this day.” The famous king’s tomb was a well-known place in Jerusalem – any listener could go there. So the psalm about the Holy One who would not see decay could not have been about David. It was about the one whose tomb, also near Jerusalem and just as easy to check, had been empty for seven weeks. An occupied tomb against an empty tomb. Peter sums up the whole sermon with the statement: “God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ!” The outpouring of the Spirit itself, Peter says, is the visible proof. The exalted Jesus “has poured out what you now see and hear.” The gift of the Spirit is not a decoration for a devout gathering. It is physical evidence that Someone has taken the throne.

sections.heading: What Shall We Do?
paragraphs: The crowd reacts the way every speaker would wish: “they were cut to the heart” and asked a practical question: “Brothers, what shall we do?” Peter’s answer is as simple as emergency instructions – repent, be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. Right after that comes a sentence that opens the door wider than anyone understood that day: “This promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off.” To all who are far off – that sentence takes in all the events described in the book of Acts: Samaria, an Ethiopian court official, a Roman centurion, and pagan cities no one in that crowd had ever heard of. It is also worth noticing whom Peter does not accuse. He speaks bluntly about Jerusalem’s guilt, but when he warns them to be saved from “this corrupt generation,” he draws the line not between nations. In the language of the time, a corrupt generation meant everyone who rejects God’s rescue, whatever their origin. The dividing line does not run between Jew and Greek but through the middle of every heart. That day about three thousand people were baptized. A church that fit into one room in the morning would not have fit into any building in Jerusalem by evening.

Right away Luke shows what these people did the next day and the days after: “They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer.” Four pillars, no fireworks. The newborn church did not live from one high to the next – it lived by a rhythm of teaching, a shared table, and prayer. It broke bread from house to house “with gladness and sincerity of heart” and shared its possessions with anyone in need. In this description there is also a sentence that ought to put every growth strategy to shame: “And the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved.” It was God who added people. The community only had to be a place people could join.

sections.heading: The News Traveled on Its Own
paragraphs: With the passing of years, one more thing becomes visible. Among Peter’s listeners Luke names visitors from Rome. The pilgrims who had come for the feast went back home afterward, and some of them went home baptized. Most likely that is exactly how the gospel reached the capital of the empire. No apostle brought it, no missionary sent by headquarters, but nameless people who had experienced something in Jerusalem and could not keep quiet about it. When Paul writes his Letter to the Romans a quarter of a century later, he will address it to a congregation that may well have had its beginnings among the pilgrims who were in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost. The church’s first missionary network turned out to be the roads home of ordinary people. That is a lesson for every congregation waiting for a salaried specialist before it does mission. From day one, the Spirit has preferred to use ordinary people on the roads of their everyday lives.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: Our series is called “There Is Hope,” and today’s story shows where hope gets its legs. The truth of the resurrection had already existed for fifty days before anyone spoke of it in public. The news was true, but it was locked in a room with frightened people. It took the Spirit to turn knowledge into courage and a handful of people into a movement. The lesson we can draw from this story is that the church usually lacks neither information nor arguments. What it lacks is fire, and we may pray for fire, because it has been promised. It is also worth paying attention to language. The miracle of Pentecost went out to meet the listeners – everyone understood everything. The uncomfortable question for us as a community is this: when an outsider walks into our gathering, do they hear “the wonders of God” in words they understand, or an insiders’ dialect? Another thing worth stressing concerns Peter himself. The Lord entrusted the first sermon in the church’s history to a man fresh from a public humiliation, as if to settle once and for all the question of who qualifies and who doesn’t. Let us also look at the phrase “to all who are far off.” On the day the church was born, God wrote into its birth certificate people who were not yet in the room. A community that lives only for those already present is disowning its own birth certificate.
